note.headline: Meta keeps growing sales, but thinner margins and cash flow keep us waiting

summary.thesis: Meta's sales are growing fast, but higher spending has cut its operating margin and free cash flow, so the price already assumes a recovery the numbers don't yet show.
summary.decision: Long-term: wait. Swing: wait. The stock is mid-range with resistance just above, and the margin question won't be answered before the 2027-01-27 report.
summary.act_at: 591.53 support for the chart; 475.85 for value

note.happening: META closed at 623.61, down 0.82% on the day. It sits below its falling 20-day average (640.44), its 50-day average (679.07) and, just barely, its 200-day average (630.5), so the chart is a sideways range. There is no new news since the last note, and the next earnings report is on 2027-01-27.
note.business: Demand looks healthy. Trailing revenue rose to 241.6B from 189.5B (27.53% growth), and gross margin is still 81.03%. Two things have weakened. Growth is slowing: the latest quarter grew 26.07% versus 33.08% two quarters ago. Profit per dollar of sales is also falling: operating margin dropped to 32.86% from 43.23%, and trailing free cash flow (cash left after running the business and investing in it) fell to 28.6B from 44.8B, an 11.86% margin. R&D now takes 31.68% of revenue and stock-based pay takes 11.15%. The filings flag that profit per share is lagging sales and that last quarter missed forecasts by 29%. The lower margins are reported to come from heavy spending on AI infrastructure (general knowledge). That spending could pay off later, but it hasn't shown up in the numbers yet. The balance sheet is not the problem: debt is 83.7B against 11.2B of cash, net cash is -1.2B, and available liquidity is 82.4B. Shareholders are barely diluted (0.04% a year). The $14.2M insider sale outside pre-set plans affects sentiment and governance, not the business. What's at risk is margins and cash generation. Demand is not at risk.

worth.text: The methods disagree widely, and one assumption explains most of the gap: how much cash Meta will generate. The cash-flow model (DCF) starts from today's depressed free cash flow of 28.6B. It values the stock at 248.92 (bear), 381.85 (base) and 521.31 (bull), all below the 623.61 price. To justify today's price, free cash flow would need to start growing about 37.1% a year. That is above the model's 30% cap, which gives 480.09. Valued on sales, the stock looks normal. Its price-to-sales ratio of 6.6 is close to the peer median of 6.5, it is 0.97 versus peers after adjusting for growth, and it sits at the 38th percentile of its own 5-year history. Meta's own sales-multiple history implies 475.85 to 881.21, with a midpoint of 707.21. The trailing P/E is 21.3. A sales-based value assumes margins return to normal, and a cash-based value assumes they don't. Our range runs from the low end of the sales history (475.85), which is near the DCF value at 30% growth, to the sales-history midpoint (707.21). Today's price is inside that range, but in the lower half, and only because we credit a recovery that hasn't happened yet.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow recovers toward the earlier 44.8B as the spending pays off, instead of staying near 28.6B.

bull: Sales are still compounding: trailing revenue rose to 241.6B from 189.5B, growth of 27.53%, with a 3-year growth rate of 23.92%.
The sales multiple isn't stretched: price-to-sales of 6.6 is near the peer median of 6.5, 0.97 versus peers after adjusting for growth, and at the 38th percentile of its own 5-year range.
If margins recover, the sales-history midpoint of 707.21 sits above today's 623.61, and gross margin is still a high 81.03%.
bear: Operating margin fell to 32.86% from 43.23%, and free cash flow fell to 28.6B from 44.8B.
The price implies about 37.1% starting cash-flow growth. Even at the 30% cap the DCF gives only 480.09, and if operating margin slipped to 24% it would give 246.18.
Growth is slowing (26.07% last quarter versus 33.08% two quarters ago), and the last quarter missed forecasts by 29%.
